evaluation.positioning_hook: A suicidal foster teen in 1976 is sent by Jesus to spend one night with Janis Joplin, Jimi Hendrix, and Jim Morrison, and discovers his dead mother’s guitar may be the key to choosing life.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The hook is immediately legible and emotionally accessible: a damaged teen, iconic dead musicians, Christmas, and a life-or-death choice. The audience is real and the premise is easy to sell, but the spiritual/fantasy register and period music rights narrow the lane from broad four-quadrant to specialty prestige.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands fast and stays clear: Sage dies, meets Jesus, gets three spirit guides, and spends the night with legendary musicians before deciding whether to live. The script keeps the rules simple enough to track while layering in the mother/guitar mystery.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Sage has a strong wounded-teen engine, and the trio of Janis/Jimi/Jim each have distinct comic and emotional flavors. The characters are memorable, though Sage’s interiority is more reactive than deeply singular for much of the piece.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a big swing by turning a suicide intervention into a Christmas fantasia with dead rock icons as spirit guides. The voice is committed and unusual, and the Aisling framing device gives it a storybook register that feels authored rather than generic.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story has a clear clock and a strong sequence engine once Sage enters the afterlife/guide framework. It does occasionally linger in explanatory dialogue, but the guitar, the birthday deadline, and the reveal of the mother keep the momentum alive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The central idea is fresh and instantly graspable: a boy who has no attachment to life is forced to confront meaning through music, myth, and the dead. The final reveal that the Christmas Nun is his mother gives the premise an emotional inevitability that feels earned.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The afterlife rules, the contract language, the spirit-guide bureaucracy, and the 1970s music-club world all create usable texture. The world is specific and story-generating, though it remains more symbolic than fully lived-in.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific tonal blend: earnest, whimsical, profane, and devotional all at once. The contrast between Aisling’s lyrical narration, Jesus’s dry bureaucracy, and the rock-star banter gives it a hard-to-copy identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the fantasy setup is a real meditation on attachment, self-worth, and the stories we inherit from parents. The mother reveal and the contract logic suggest more emotional depth than the surface adventure initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Sage/Janis/Jimi/Jim dynamic generates constant friction, comedy, and emotional triangulation, and Jesus adds a separate authority lane. Any two or three of them in a room create playable scenes, which is a real asset for the feature.

lead_characters.name: Sage Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 14, white/Anglo, foster child, emotionally isolated, working-class, California teen.
lead_characters.hook: A bruised, defensive foster kid with no real attachments, Sage is all sharp edges and buried need. He enters the story ready to die, then gets dragged through a supernatural Christmas night that forces him to confront the one thing he has never allowed himself: the possibility that his life might matter.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young River Phoenix in My Own Private Idaho or a teen lead in The Perks of Being a Wallflower — a role that lets an actor play numbness, anger, vulnerability, and a gradual emotional thaw in one arc.

lead_characters.name: Aisling
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s-30s, Irish, convent-trained, spiritually luminous, physically fragile.
lead_characters.hook: Aisling is the storybook narrator and emotional bridge between the convent past and Sage’s present. She speaks like a folk tale come alive, but the script reveals her as a woman who has lived through the same choice architecture she is now trying to explain to Sage.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Saoirse Ronan in Brooklyn or Emily Watson in Hilary and Jackie a chance to carry warmth, mystery, and emotional authority at once — a performance built on voice and presence as much as plot.

lead_characters.name: Jesus
lead_characters.demographics: Male, ageless/appears 30s, divine figure in human form, casual, witty, authoritative.
lead_characters.hook: Jesus is less a solemn deity than a dry, overworked caseworker for souls, which is exactly why he works. He’s funny, patient, and a little exasperated, but he also carries the story’s moral weight and the final decision point.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Alan Rickman in Dogma or Morgan Freeman in Bruce Almighty — a role that lets an actor play authority, wit, and spiritual gravity without losing charm.

lead_characters.name: Janis Joplin
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 20s/appears as iconic 1960s rock star, white, flamboyant, emotionally open.
lead_characters.hook: Janis is the emotional heart of the trio: impulsive, affectionate, funny, and unexpectedly maternal. She gives Sage the first real sense that he is seen, and she’s the one who can turn the room from chaos into grace.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Kate Winslet in Eternal Sunshine or Melissa McCarthy in St. Vincent a chance to be both comic and deeply tender — a performance with warmth, swagger, and a late-scene emotional payoff.

lead_characters.name: Jim Morrison
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s/appears as iconic 1960s rock star, white, charismatic, volatile, poetic.
lead_characters.hook: Morrison is the seductive, slightly dangerous intellect in the room, equal parts shaman, performer, and self-mythologizer. He can pivot from comic vanity to genuine compassion, which makes him the trio’s most unstable emotional weather system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that let Val Kilmer in The Doors or Joaquin Phoenix in Walk the Line inhabit charisma with menace — a chance to play iconography, ego, and vulnerability in the same breath.

lead_characters.name: Jimi Hendrix
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s/appears as iconic 1960s rock star, Black, electric, playful, mercurial.
lead_characters.hook: Hendrix is the wild card: funny, impatient, musically gifted, and always one beat away from chaos. He brings the script its most anarchic energy, but he also becomes part of the emotional argument for staying alive.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jamie Foxx in Ray or André 3000 in Idlewild a chance to perform charisma as movement, rhythm, and attitude — a role that lives in the body as much as the dialogue.

lead_characters.name: Wallace March
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, white, club owner, practical, decent, quietly burdened.
lead_characters.hook: Wallace is the grounded adult in the real world, the man whose guitar and club become the physical bridge between Sage’s spiritual night and his waking life. He’s not flashy, but he matters because he’s the first living person to offer Sage a nonjudgmental hand.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is solid character-actor territory in the lane of Richard Jenkins in The Visitor or Jeffrey Wright in Basquiat — a role that plays restraint, decency, and emotional subtext.

lead_characters.name: Suzy
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 15, white, street-smart, sexually confident, music-scene adjacent.
lead_characters.hook: Suzy is the gateway into the club world: brash, funny, and more perceptive than she first appears. She clocks Sage quickly, then keeps nudging him toward the social and sensual world he has never really entered.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Jennifer Lawrence in Winter’s Bone or Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 a chance to be tough, funny, and emotionally readable at once.

lead_characters.name: Mother Superior
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, Irish, convent authority figure, stern but humane.
lead_characters.hook: Mother Superior is the moral custodian of the convent scenes, equal parts discipline and mercy. She’s the one who understands the room’s miracle before anyone else does, and she gives the opening and closing frame its authority.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a veteran actor the same kind of scene-stealing dignity as Maggie Smith in The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel — controlled, dry, and quietly moving.

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: mostly interiors with a few key exteriors
notable_requirements: period wardrobe and set dressing for both 1960s and 1970s

technical.vfx_details: Soul separation, magical parchment scroll, apparition/manifestation of Jesus and the three musicians, and a few stylized supernatural transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: practical effects for soul/body separation, clock and parchment gags, and apparition transitions.

rights_flags.detail: The Doors' 'Break on Through (To the Other Side)', Led Zeppelin's 'Stairway to Heaven', 'Happy Birthday', 'Silent Night', and 'Jingle Bells' are all plot-embedded or performance-critical.
Jesus Christ is depicted as a speaking character.
Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, and Jim Morrison are depicted as speaking characters.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical with strong streaming afterlife

budget.note: The period convent, 1970s club, and supernatural effects keep this above a simple contained indie, but the location count stays manageable and the set pieces are character-driven rather than action-heavy.

casting.note: Sage needs a young actor who can carry suicidal despair and comic wonder, while the Hendrix/Joplin/Morrison trio has to feel iconic rather than impressionistic. Jesus also needs a performer who can play authority without flattening the humor.

development.note: The script’s voice is distinctive, but the tonal balance between sacred, profane, and whimsical is delicate, and the Jesus/rock-star framework will be a taste-driven conversation for buyers.

comp_set.title: Defending Your Life
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the afterlife-as-bureaucracy structure and the emotional premise of a soul being asked to justify its life.

comp_set.title: The Fisher King
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the blend of spiritual longing, urban myth, and wounded characters searching for redemption through connection.

comp_set.title: Almost Famous
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on music-world texture, youthful longing, and the emotional power of being briefly accepted by a band of larger-than-life personalities.

comp_set.title: Dogma
comp_set.why_it_comps: The Jesus-as-character lane and the irreverent-but-sincere spiritual comedy register are close cousins.

comp_set.title: A Christmas Carol
comp_set.why_it_comps: The ghostly visitation structure and redemption-through-vision framework map cleanly onto the script’s Christmas-night intervention.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like prestige fantasy with music, heart, and a strong emotional payoff — especially viewers drawn to spiritually inflected coming-of-age stories.
audience_target.demographics: 18-54, skewing female but with real male appeal through the music-icon hook; strongest with educated, culture-literate audiences and music fans.

budget_tier.note: A modest period build, a handful of interiors, and moderate supernatural effects keep this in indie-feature territory despite the music-icon casting and clearance considerations.

lane_fit.lane: prestige fantasy drama with music DNA
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of elevated, emotionally sincere fantasy with a strong soundtrack identity. The hook is unusual enough to stand out, but the emotional core is accessible enough to sell to buyers looking for awards-adjacent crowd appeal.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The premise resolves around Sage’s one-night choice and does not naturally open a sequel or spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A one-sentence hook with real emotional lift
strengths.what_it_means: This is easy to pitch, easy to remember, and easy to market because the premise fuses a life-or-death teen story with iconic music mythology. That makes it attractive to specialty buyers and streamer teams looking for something that feels both original and emotionally legible.
strengths.evidence: Sage’s suicide attempt, Jesus’s intervention, and the arrival of Janis, Jimi, and Jim all happen within the first act.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The trio creates a built-in ensemble engine
strengths.what_it_means: Janis, Jimi, and Jim are not just cameos; they generate banter, conflict, and emotional triangulation that can carry long scenes. That gives the film a playable cast dynamic that actors and directors can get excited about.
strengths.evidence: Their arguments over Sage, the pills, and the meaning of the night repeatedly shift the scene energy.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The Christmas setting gives the story a clean commercial wrapper
strengths.what_it_means: The holiday frame makes the movie feel seasonal without turning it into a conventional family title, which broadens its programming value. Buyers can position it as a counter-programming Christmas release with heart and edge.
strengths.evidence: The story is explicitly set on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, with repeated use of carols and miracle imagery.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The mother reveal gives the fantasy an emotional payoff
strengths.what_it_means: The final connection between the Christmas Nun and Sage’s mother turns the supernatural premise into a personal inheritance story. That kind of reveal gives the film a stronger aftertaste and helps justify the spiritual conceit to skeptical buyers.
strengths.evidence: Aisling is revealed as Sage’s mother, and the guitar becomes the bridge between them.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a distinctive verbal identity that can help it stand out in a crowded indie marketplace. Buyers looking for authored material will respond to a piece that sounds like itself on the page.
strengths.evidence: Aisling’s lyrical narration, the comic Jesus, and the profane rock-star dialogue all share a coherent, stylized register.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Music is not decoration; it is story engine
strengths.what_it_means: The songs are tied to memory, identity, and the emotional turn of the plot, which makes the soundtrack feel integral rather than ornamental. That gives the film a strong hook for music-minded buyers and audience word of mouth.
strengths.evidence: The guitar, 'Happy Birthday,' 'Silent Night,' and 'Break on Through' all drive key turns.

whats_special.headline: This is a highly ownable prestige-fantasy feature: a suicidal teen, a Christmas-night spiritual quest, and the dead icons of rock music all in one package. The concept is commercial because it’s instantly pitchable, the cast dynamic is actor-friendly, and the contained period footprint keeps it inside a realistic indie budget lane.

items.area: The music clearances are the first buyer conversation.
items.detail: The script is built around plot-critical use of The Doors, Led Zeppelin, and multiple carols, plus performance moments that depend on those songs landing. That means sync cost and rights availability are not incidental; they are part of the greenlight math.

The script asks buyers to embrace a very specific blend of reverence, irreverence, and pop-mythology, and that will not be universal. For some executives it will read as inspired; for others it will be a hard tonal ask before they even get to the emotional payoff.

items.area: Sage’s interior arc is sometimes carried by explanation.
items.detail: A lot of the emotional logic is delivered through Aisling’s narration, Jesus’s exposition, and the spirit-guide dialogue rather than through action alone. That keeps the premise clear, but it also means the lead’s transformation is occasionally more spoken than dramatized.

items.area: The period and iconography narrow the casting lane.
items.detail: Sage has to read as fragile, angry, and sympathetic in the same frame, and the three musician roles need recognizable charisma without becoming impersonations. That combination narrows the pool and makes attachment more consequential than the page count suggests.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is clearance and taste: the movie lives on named songs, named icons, and a very specific spiritual-comic tone that will be a yes for some buyers and a pass for others. Beyond that, the lead role and period styling are manageable, but they do require a cast and package that can sell the premise fast.
